The Grain Gathering 2026: What a Home Baker Brings Back from the Breadlab

  • Notes from the back of the bread truck.
  • By Maurizio Leo
  • Updated: Aug 7, 2026
  • 32 Comments

Post might include affiliate links. See policy.

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 8:26
Instaread

I was riding about five feet off the ground in the back of a truck, sharing the bed with a bread oven, mill, mixer, and workbench—all powered by a solar array on the roof. By day three of the Grain Gathering, this seemed like a perfectly reasonable place to be.

Marc Benoit built the mobile bakery and mill to shorten the chain from field to loaf and to push more of what a loaf costs back to the farmer who grew the grain in the first place. The truck buildout was a standout, but it was the crew—Marc, Baylin Speidel, and Thomas Vroom—that made the weekend for me. We milled and baked with Moon Family Farms’ Hollis, Chimacum Confluence, and Palouse Heritage Elwha River Spelt: twenty-odd loaves, three large-format focaccia, an armada of baguettes, and bialys topped with sesame and roasted vegetables. And the oven (a workhorse RackMaster) was still at temp when we quit.

When I signed up for my first Grain Gathering, my worry was that it would lean too far into farming and wheat breeding—that it’d be industry folks talking to industry folks, with no place for a home baker. Then I started hopping between conversations and found bakers of every kind, from “two-loafer” home bakers to pros, geeking out about falling numbers, mixing techniques, and how best to run a community bakery.

But everything these people breed, grow, and mill ends up, eventually, in somebody’s oven, and often an oven like mine. The chain from breeder to farmer to miller to baker is longer than I had appreciated. For three days, every pair of hands in the chain stood under one tent. I’ve spent many years at the last link; it was something else to meet the rest.

The Grain Gathering is less a conference than a congregation of the grain-obsessed under this year’s theme, “Nourishing Communities.” The WSU Breadlab and the WSDA hosted the event July 19–21 in Washington’s Skagit Valley—the first gathering in eight years.

Over those three days, in and out of talks, masterclasses, and wheat fields, I kept running into the same few ideas.

Who Gets Paid for a Loaf of Bread

An “artisanal” loaf of sourdough bread runs $6 to $12 (and maybe higher?) these days. You could argue that bread is a staple and should be priced as one, that is, cheap enough for anyone to afford. While I agree, there’s a lot more happening in the field. The commodity grain system takes in grain and anonymizes it: all wheat turned into a single, static element with no identity and no price differential. Great for feeding the masses, which is important, but once the grain hits the pile, the care, attention to soil health, and the farmer’s growing obsession go unpaid.

The mobile mill and bakery is an unbroken chain of custody as grain goes in with a farmer’s name and comes out as bread that can be directly traced back to its grower. Think about the novelty of that for a moment: the farmer finally gets a spot on the bag alongside the baker.

And milling and baking in one place means the operator keeps the miller’s, distributor’s, and retailer’s margins. Put a trailer like this in the hands of the farmer, and suddenly it becomes a revenue stream that otherwise scatters down the chain.

As a home baker, when you buy identity-preserved grain directly from a farm or small mill—better yet, milling it fresh at home—you’re playing the same game to compress the supply chain.

What a Wheat Breeder Optimizes For, and Why Grocery Flour Tastes the Way It Does

Almost every wheat variety grown is a pile of decisions someone made about what mattered at the time: yield, uniformity, disease resistance, baking performance, and ease of harvest. But what’s missing from that list? Flavor and nutrition.

This came up in nearly every conversation I had with breeders and bakers alike: how do you grow grain that still checks the farmer’s boxes (yield and performance) and get flavor and nutrition back into the loaf? Certainly what I’m always harping about—proper fermentation—but also using more whole grains and, frankly, the right grains to begin with.

The WSU Breadlab’s answer is to put flavor and nutrition on the scorecard. They breed varieties like Skagit 1109, Salish Blue, and Ruth (on my list to source and test!), to name a few, suited to thrive in specific growing conditions—not all conditions. Then they do the part most skip: mill and bake the candidates to see how they perform in a loaf.

In the home kitchen, this means you can have a bag labeled with a variety name and unique baking characteristics, because it’s precisely the opposite of the anonymous pile. The flavor has a name, and so does the farmer who grew it.

What Changes Back Home

It’s easy to come away beaming with energy from three days of fervent fermentation, claiming you’re going to overhaul your entire baking life.

To make a difference, it doesn’t have to be a complete upheaval of all you know and do. It can start small: swap one of your grains for an identity-preserved variety like Ruth, or source some grain directly from a farmer and mill it yourself.

If you traced my baking from start until now, you’d spot a trend toward more whole grains, more named varieties, and more freshly milled flour. Not everything I bake is along these lines (there’s a case to be made for high-quality sifted flour, too), but my goal is to keep pushing this evolution in my baking farther and farther.

Not because I feel like I “should,” but because I’m after the best flavor, the highest nutrition. And just maybe, with the right grain, you don’t have to choose between them.

The People

There were so many talented, passionate, and accomplished folks at the gathering it’s impossible for me to recount all our conversations and happenstance encounters, but here are a few:

Baylin Speidel, Head Baker, Chimacum: baking alongside you is always a pleasure, as was the running argument over why Star Trek is the work of a genius.

Thomas Vroom, who bakes on Vashon Island: we finally meet. I’m coming to see that island soon.

Marc Benoit: part madman, part renaissance man. The trailer speaks for itself, but thank you for who it speaks for—the farmers, millers, and everyone else who makes bread possible.

Crystie and Keith Kisler of Chimacum Valley Grainery: always inspiring and ever positive. Growing, milling, (and baking with and malting and…) some of the best grain anywhere.

Kevin Morse, Meech Crowley, and Jon Feldman of Cairnspring Mills: thank you for the mill tour, and for getting Skagit grain into kitchens like mine.

Andrew Heyn and Blair Marvin of Elmore Mountain Bread: I’ve followed your baking as long as I’ve been a baker. Talking milling, growing, and community with you both was a long time coming.

Jeffrey Hamelman: your book has been a north star since my earliest bakes. Meeting you continues to confirm everything it suggested about its author.

Andrew Ross: we finally meet! So great to talk wheat, buckwheat, bread, and pizza with you. Inspiring as always.

Katie Phelan: my handwriting-obsessed friend. Thanks for the chats about France and wood-fired baking—until the next adventure.

Brandon Buza: always a pleasure traveling and baking with you. Next trip, we’re capping the luggage count.

Cat Cox of Country Bird Bakery: thanks for our talks around community and what it means to make bread people love.

And thanks to Sandy A. and Ran C. for the help in the bakery and the hikes, and to everyone who stopped by the truck for a slice and a hello.

Parting

The Grain Gathering surprised me. But the theme had it right, too: it nourished. What I found was a congregation of the grain-obsessed, focused on feeding the people who eat their bread, whether they bake two loaves at a time or a hundred.

I don’t have a mobile bakery and mill, but what I do have is a small electric mill on the counter. When I flip the switch, the flour it makes comes from farmers I’ve now met, baked beside, and toured a wheat field with. After three days in the Skagit with this bunch of grain-heads, it really does seem like a perfectly reasonable place to end up.

    This confirms my experience: for years I thought AP flour felt silky and soft whenever I handled it for baking. Two years ago I began buying whole grains (some from local farmers) to mill & bake our two loaves a week & pretty much everything else that called for flour.

    This past winter I baked something that relied on a nationally hailed high quality AP flour. I was alarmed that it felt artificial. There was no sweet aroma, it felt dry and friable, & I imagined it must have an additive or something to prevent clumping. Wow, what a wake up call.

    Home ground (local if possible, or sourced from reliable farms online) makes an enormous difference. Home milling is not at all difficult or time consuming. The difference is real, and getting whole grains from local or regional farmers is one more way to support a healthy community.

    1. Maurizio Leo says:
      August 19, 2026 at 3:04 pm

      Yes, this came up quite a bit at the Grain Gathering! Beyond Barton Springs Mill and Janie’s Mill (both great), look into Camas Country Mill in Oregon, Bluebird Grain Farms in Washington (they focus on heritage varieties like einkorn and emmer), and Sunrise Flour Mill in Minnesota, which specializes in heritage Turkey Red. Grist & Toll in California is another good one. The Bread Lab at WSU also maintains lists of regional growers working with older varieties. You’re right that many farms only label by class, so asking directly about varieties is usually the way to go. The good news is more farmers are bringing back these older wheats every year. Thanks for the comments, Bethany!

  8. Cate says:
    August 7, 2026 at 12:30 pm

    Over the past six months, I’ve gradually replaced commercial steel roller-milled wheat flour with stone-ground and Unifine-milled flours from local mills that either grow and mill wheat in my home state, purchase wheat from farmers within my state, or are family farms that grow, mill, and sell their flour directly to consumers.

    The learning curve involved in working with very fresh flours—some whole wheat, some high extraction—milled using methods that preserve more of the wheat kernel’s flavor and nutritional properties has been steep and challenging to navigate.

    Things progressed well in the beginning as I gradually transitions from 100% commercially produced flour to 70:30 commercial flour:stoneground/unifine.

    My initial approach of simply tweaking my existing formulas and mixing methods collapsed when I changed the commercial flour in my blend with 75% extraction local wheat and locally milled flour. Instead of my usual big-bellied batards, I pulled loaf after loaf of dense, flat disks from the oven. So I set aside everything I understood and used with commercial flour formulas and started from scratch.

    I stopped with blending for now. I am now testing hydration tolerance of the wheat flours individually, using 50 g of flour and evaluating how the unleavened dough develops with added water from 65% to 85% in 5% increments. I am also sieving 100% whole wheat flour to extraction rates of 75%, 80%, and 85%, then testing each extraction level separately.

    With commercial roller-milled flour, I rarely had to consider anything beyond protein content when deciding how much water a flour could absorb and still produce the necessary gluten strength.

    With both the local stone ground wheat flour and the unifine milled heritage wheat flours I find protein content doesn’t tell me much about the flours’ potential. Instead, I have had to learn how the wheat variety, milling method, extraction rate, and the number of days since milling all interact to determine how much water the flour can absorb and how much gluten strength the flour can ultimately develop.

    Reply

      For example, I’ve found that using Azure Ultra-Unifine Unbleached Bread Flour, which has approximately 88% extraction, the ideal hydration level is usually 2-3% higher (USUALLY-lol). However, I’m still working on perfecting it when adding other flours, such as Unifine whole-grain spelt.
